column2: England's most famous royal dynasty (Henry VIII and his six wives, Elizabeth I).
Fortress, palace and London's most famous prison, where the ravens reside.
A pirate — one with a royal licence, if you please.
The queen's pirate who smashed the Invincible Armada.
The name of London's oldest psychiatric hospital, turned byword for utter chaos.
A campaigner for women's right to vote (the sort from Mary Poppins).
The ancient stone circle on Salisbury Plain, whose mystery remains unsolved.
The leader of the English Revolution, the country's only Lord Protector.
The grim yet instantly recognisable symbol of the French Revolution; an invention its creator, a physician, considered the most humane form of execution.
A soldier of the French royal guard, made famous by Alexandre Dumas.
The Belgian village turned byword for total and final defeat — the site of Napoleon's last battle.
The church court of medieval Europe, hunting heretics and witches.
The famous Florentine banking dynasty that patronised Leonardo da Vinci and Michelangelo.
A French surname turned byword for short men with outsized ambitions.
The joking label for the poor revolutionaries of Paris, who wore long trousers instead of the aristocratic knee breeches (culottes).
A cattle herder of the Wild West, the lead of every western.
The 16th president of the USA, who abolished slavery and wore the famous top hat.
An underground liquor trader of the American Prohibition years of the 1920s.
The name turned byword through the great northern gold rush described by Jack London.
The best-known American gangster of the Chicago mafia era.
The revolver that 'levelled all men' in the Wild West.
The name given to the first English settlers who sailed to America aboard the Mayflower and began the Thanksgiving tradition.
The forest hiding the noble outlaw of King Richard the Lionheart's day.
One of the two peoples whose rivalry drives the plot of Ivanhoe.
The grim nickname of the elusive Victorian London murderer who was never caught.
The name of London's police force, made legendary by Arthur Conan Doyle.
The harsh institution for the poor in nineteenth-century England, described by Charles Dickens — via the boy who asked for more.
One of the two warring houses of the Wars of the Roses, which inspired Game of Thrones.
One of the two warring houses of the Wars of the Roses, which inspired Game of Thrones.
The mighty 'Red Cardinal' who ruled France under Louis XIII and crossed swords with d'Artagnan.
The celebrated spy and adventuress of Dumas's novel (the word itself is an English noble title, turned byword).
The castle-prison on an island off Marseille, from which the Count of Monte Cristo made his daring escape.
The Cathedral of Our Lady in Paris.
The hunchback of the Paris cathedral, invented by Victor Hugo.
A French Protestant of the religious wars and the St Bartholomew's Day massacre.
The Spanish conqueror of the Americas, a seeker of El Dorado and the Inca gold.
The national hero of Italy, fighter for its unification — and, in Britain, a currant biscuit of the same name.
The scornful name Southerners gave the Northerners in the American Civil War.
The extinct Indian tribe turned byword thanks to Fenimore Cooper's novel — hence 'the last of'.
The chief keeper of the law in Wild West towns, with a star on his chest.
The great river of paddle steamers and of Tom Sawyer and Huckleberry Finn on their raft.
The vast estate of the American South where cotton was grown before slavery was abolished.
The multi-seat mail carriage forever attacked by bandits in the classic westerns.
A Caribbean pirate who plundered Spanish galleons — the sort made famous by Captain Blood.
The legendary magic sword of King Arthur from the Round Table legends, bound to the right of supreme power over Britain.
Walter Scott's adventure novel, set in England in the reign of Richard I the Lionheart.
The American jazz composer and pianist, leader of his own jazz orchestra, among the best-known jazz musicians of the twentieth century.
The surname of the celebrated American-Mexican guitarist who fused rock with Latin rhythms.
The popular-music genre that took shape in the USA in the late 1940s and early 1950s and became the early foundation of all rock music.
The African-American musical genre and form, arising in the second half of the nineteenth century in the American South from work songs, spirituals and ballads.
The famous Swedish pop group formed in 1972 and named after the first letters of the members' names.
The revolutionary song of the French Revolution and the national anthem of France.
The living time machine and spaceship of Doctor Who, built by the Time Lords of Gallifrey — famously bigger on the inside.
